subject: history

moments.title: Germ theory established
moments.body: Pasteur's work on fermentation (1857) and the swan-neck flask experiments (1859) disprove spontaneous generation. He shows micro-organisms cause disease in silkworms, in beer, in wine. Pasteurisation (heat treatment to kill microbes) is patented in 1865.
moments.takeaway: Germ theory replaced miasma. The implication for medicine — sterile technique, infection control — was enormous.

moments.title: Lister and antiseptic surgery
moments.body: Lister applies Pasteur's theory to surgery. Carbolic acid spray and dressings reduce post-operative infections from around 50% to single digits. Lister's 1867 Lancet paper is initially met with scepticism — Florence Nightingale was sceptical for years.
moments.takeaway: Surgery moved from a near-death sentence to a routine procedure. The hospital itself was reconceived from a death-house to a place of cure.

moments.title: Anthrax and rabies vaccines
moments.body: 1881: public demonstration at Pouilly-le-Fort — vaccinated sheep survive anthrax exposure, unvaccinated die. 1885: Pasteur treats 9-year-old Joseph Meister, bitten by a rabid dog, with an attenuated rabies vaccine. Meister survives.

quote.text: Chance favours only the prepared mind.
quote.attrib: Louis Pasteur, lecture at the University of Lille, 1854

moments.takeaway: The Pasteur Institute (Paris, founded 1887) became a global model for medical research institutions.

now.title: Germ theory's reach
now.body: All modern medicine — from hand-washing to vaccination to antibiotic prescription — rests on the framework Pasteur established. Robert Koch's parallel work in Germany (Koch's postulates, identification of TB and cholera bacilli in 1882-83) completed the foundation. Microbiome research now extends the picture: bacteria are not just pathogens but constitutive of human biology.
now.open_questions: How does the microbiome reframe germ theory? The idea that all bacteria are enemies has been replaced by a far more complex picture of host-microbe symbiosis. This shifts ideas about antibiotic use, hygiene and chronic disease.

reflection: The 1860s saw medicine reconceived from a humoural to a microbial framework. Almost everything taught in a modern medical school descends from that shift. The change was contested and slow — but once accepted, it remade clinical practice within a generation.
